CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Reading — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the reading club habit: the child picks the book, the grown-up brings the voices, and prediction turns every page turn into a game.

What is this?

Reading club is a daily story appointment — same cushion, same ten minutes, book chosen by the child. The card’s printed skills are Imagine & Learn: the pictures the mind builds and the facts it collects along the way.

What does it mean?

Choice is the engine: children who pick their own books read longer and ask to re-read, and re-reading is where the real learning hides — the second pass notices everything the first missed. Predicting the next page trains comprehension before the words are even decoded.

What does the child need to know?

A book basket with three to five choices, a reading spot with the good light, and voices: one for the bear, one for the wind, one whisper for the secret pages.

Why this matters

Daily reading is the single highest-leverage habit in early childhood — vocabulary, attention, empathy and school readiness all ride on it. The ritual matters as much as the book: same time, same spot, same voices.

What it teaches

Vocabulary growth, story sequencing, prediction skills, listening stamina, print awareness (text runs left to right, pages turn one way), and the book-love that outlasts the lesson.

Words to learn

storypagepredictcharacterbeginningendlibraryfavoritechapter

Say this to your child

“"Reading club! Bring me the basket — you pick today’s book. Let’s guess from the cover: what happens? ... Now listen to the bear’s voice. And STOP — what happens next?"”

Step by step

  1. The basket comes out; the child chooses today’s book with full ceremony.
  2. Read the cover: title, author, and a guess from the picture of what happens.
  3. Read with voices — slow down at the good parts, pause before the turn.
  4. Play pause-and-predict: stop one page early and let everyone guess the ending.
  5. Close with the re-read offer: same book again is ALWAYS allowed — favorites are how readers are made.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the book is open to a castle page and held toward the viewer — the picture inside the book is doing its job: the reader is already inside the story.

Ask your child

"What do you think happens next?" "Which voice should the wolf have?" "Who was your favorite character?" "Should we read it again tomorrow?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may memorize whole pages and recite them (real reading’s first draft), demand the same book for two weeks (excellent), or read to the pets — audiences of fur are traditional.

Out in the real world

Authors, librarians, teachers and podcasters all live on stories read aloud first. Every big reader started in a lap with a book they chose themselves.

Try it together

Story detectives: after the book, three quick questions — who, what happened first, what changed? Three answers and the detective badge is earned for the day.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who chooses the book in reading club?" (the reader) "What do we do at the pause?" (predict) "How long does club last?" (ten minutes — every day)

This lesson pairs with the Reading flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
